lede: Real tables have more columns than any one question needs. `select` keeps the ones you ask for, in the order you want, and can rename them or work out new values on the way.
objectives: Pick columns by name or with `F.col` using `select`
Rename a column in the result with `alias`
Work out new columns with arithmetic such as `F.col("minutes_spent") / 60`
Write the same thing as SQL text with `selectExpr`

blocks.md:
The tables above come from a small learning platform: `learners`, the `lessons` of each course, and `attempts`, one row per try at a lesson. On this page they're loaded as DataFrames with those names, and `F` is `pyspark.sql.functions`.

`df.select(...)` gives back a **new** DataFrame with only the columns you list, in the order you list them. Every row stays, and `df` itself doesn't change.

blocks.title: Pick columns by name
blocks.note: The second result has `plan` first, because that's the order it was asked for, not the order in the table.

blocks.md: Instead of a name you can pass a column, written `F.col("name")`. A column can do more than a name can. `.alias("new_name")` gives it a new name in the result, and you can mix plain names and `F.col` in the same `select`.

blocks.title: Rename with alias
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

scores = attempts.select("attempt_id", "learner_id", F.col("score_pct").alias("score"))
scores.show()
blocks.note: Only the result has the new name. `attempts` still has its `score_pct` column.

blocks.md:
Columns work with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`, against a number or another column. The result is a new column, worked out for every row. Give it a name with `alias`, and put the arithmetic in brackets first so `alias` names the whole calculation.

If a value is missing, a calculation with it is missing too.

blocks.title: Work out a new column
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

lessons.select("title", F.col("estimated_minutes") / 60).show(3)

lessons.select("title", "estimated_minutes", (F.col("estimated_minutes") / 60).alias("hours")).show(3)
blocks.note: Without `alias`, the new column is named after the calculation: `(estimated_minutes / 60)`. Dividing with `/` always gives a `double`, even when both sides are whole numbers.

blocks.title: A column that isn't there
blocks.note: The column is called `score_pct`. Spark stops before running anything and suggests names that do exist, so the error message is worth reading.

blocks.md: `selectExpr` does the same job with SQL text: each argument is a column name or a small SQL expression, and `AS` does what `alias` does. It's handy for a quick calculation; `F.col` is easier to build up in Python as expressions grow.

blocks.title: The same with selectExpr
blocks.note: `selectExpr` gives the same result you'd get from `select` with `F.col`, `/` and `alias`.

concept.why: `select` returns exactly the columns you list, in the order you list them.

concept.prompt: Which line gives a column called `hours`?
concept.why: The calculation in brackets, then `.alias("hours")`. Without `alias` the column is called `(minutes_spent / 60)`; `select` treats text as a column name, so SQL text needs `selectExpr`; and there is no `hours` column to pick.

concept.prompt: An attempt's `minutes_spent` is missing. What is `F.col("minutes_spent") / 60` for that row?
concept.why: A calculation with a missing value is missing too. The row stays; only its value is NULL.

review: `df.select(...)` returns a new DataFrame with the columns you list, in that order. Every row stays.
Pass names like `"learner_id"` or columns like `F.col("learner_id")`, mixed as you like.
`.alias("new_name")` renames a column in the result; the original DataFrame keeps its names.
Arithmetic on columns makes a new column. Wrap it in brackets before `.alias`. `/` always gives a `double`.
A calculation with a missing value is missing.
`selectExpr` takes SQL text, with `AS` for a new name.
